title: the butter thief
hookLine: the village women bring Yashoda a long list of butter crimes, and can't stay angry
carry: lila: God comes close as a child at play

cards: A group of women stands at Yashoda's door, and they have a list. They are the gopis, the cowherd women of the village. Putana is gone, and now there's a different problem, and he's a toddler.
Butter has been disappearing all over the village. Curd too. Milk pots are broken.
And every trail leads back to this house. So they come to his mother, half laughing, half fed up, and make their case, item by item.

teach.h: THE CALVES, THE MONKEYS, THE POTS.
teach.b: Here is their list, as the Bhagavata Purana gives it. He turns the calves loose before milking time. He gets into the milk and curd, and when he's had his fill, he feeds the rest to the monkeys.
If a monkey won't eat, he breaks the pot.

teach.h: STOOLS, A MORTAR, A HOLE IN THE POT.
teach.b: People hang their pots high from the ceiling on ropes, so he drags over stools and a mortar and climbs, or makes a hole in the bottom of the pot and drinks from underneath.
In a dark storeroom he doesn't even need a lamp: the jewels he wears light the way. Then the turn.
All the while, Krishna sits beside his mother with wide, frightened eyes, the picture of a child who has never touched a pot.
The women look at that face and can't keep scolding. They laugh. And Yashoda smiles and doesn't have the heart to punish him.
Notice what kind of complaint this is. Nobody stops making butter. Nobody locks the door.
They keep coming to report him, and in the reporting they get to talk about him and be near him.
Hindus have a word for this side of God: lila, divine play. The Lord who holds the universe comes as a toddler with butter on his face, close enough to scold, to laugh at, to love.
Some devotional teachers read the stolen butter as the devotee's heart, hung up high, that he finds his way into anyway.
That's why, on Janmashtami, families set butter and sugar before baby Krishna: the thief gladly takes what's offered with love, and it comes back to them as prasad.

how: Krishna as the butter thief is a familiar figure in Hindu devotion: images of the child Krishna with butter in his hand are kept in homes and temples, many families offer him makhan mishri (butter with sugar) on Janmashtami and share it as prasad, and some communities hang pots of curd high up for teams to climb and break.

o: the butter thief gladly takes what's offered with love, and it comes back as prasad.
it's a joke about him being a thief.
games.why: the gopis kept leaving their butter out; families still offer it to him with love, and share it after as prasad.

practice: If something sweet is nearby, set a little aside before you eat: a bite, a spoonful, a piece of fruit. Many Hindu homes offer food to Krishna first, then share it as prasad.
Hold it for a moment and say his name, or, if you don't pray, simply thank whoever made it. Then eat it slowly, and let it taste like a gift instead of a snack.

orig.note: Hindi: butter thief, a name devotees use for the child Krishna.

carryVoice: Your line: lila, God comes close as a child at play. Tomorrow, his mother reaches for a rope. That's day eight hundred eighty-seven.
